profiles.meeting_scenario: At an academic medical center, the interventional oncology team is preparing to use an uncertainty-aware RF ablation planning workflow for an upcoming liver metastasis case, moving beyond retrospective simulation toward prospective clinical use. The meeting is between the lead interventional radiologist and the computational modeling lead to plan how the first case will be prepared, what materials will be produced, who will handle segmentation and optimization, and when the output must be available relative to the Monday liver tumor board and the later ablation procedure. The agenda is to select the first candidate case, confirm the vessel-aware modeling workflow, define what the planning deliverable will look like, assign responsibilities, and agree on the timeline. The expected outcome is an apparently shared plan for producing a patient-specific optimized probe placement package for the first prospective case.

members.name: Dr. Elena Markovic
members.role: Interventional Radiologist and Director of Image-Guided Oncology
members.expertise: Percutaneous liver tumor ablation, CT-guided probe placement, multidisciplinary case selection
members.background: She leads the hospital's liver ablation program, has performed more than 400 RF ablations, and regularly presents cases at the Monday 7:00 AM liver tumor board.
members.private_state: She wants the new planning approach to be usable in real clinical workflow without slowing case selection or procedure prep, and she is especially concerned that the first prospective use look polished enough for clinical colleagues to trust it.
hidden_assumptions: If a plan is said to be ready 'for Monday,' that means it can be shown in polished form at the 7:00 AM liver tumor board, not merely generated at some point that day.
When the team says the model will 'account for vessels,' that includes clinically relevant small peritumoral vessels near the lesion, even if they are not cleanly segmented as named vessels.
A 'planning packet' or 'final plan' naturally means one recommended probe trajectory set with annotated images and a brief backup option, because clinicians need a single actionable proposal.
For a first prospective case, the planning output should be available early enough to influence the board discussion about approach, not just exist before the procedure.

members.name: Dr. Noah Chen
members.role: Biomedical Engineer and Computational Modeling Lead
members.expertise: Thermal ablation simulation, uncertainty quantification, image-based optimization of probe placement
members.background: He developed the lab's RF ablation planning code, including vessel-aware heat transfer and parameter uncertainty modules, and usually supports projects through technical reports rather than direct clinical presentation materials.
members.private_state: He wants the first prospective use to be methodologically defensible and not overpromise precision, and he is trying to keep the workflow reproducible with minimal manual customization for each patient.
hidden_assumptions: If a plan is said to be ready 'for Monday,' that means the technical output files are delivered by end of day Monday unless an earlier clock time is explicitly stated.

When the model is described as 'vessel-aware,' it refers to explicitly segmented vessels above the practical resolution threshold of the pipeline, while smaller vessels are already absorbed into the background perfusion term.

A 'planning packet' or 'final plan' naturally means the optimization output bundle: several ranked feasible trajectories, uncertainty maps, and supporting technical figures rather than a single clinician-facing recommendation.
For a first prospective case, it still counts as prospective use if the output is generated before treatment as an observational aid, even if it does not shape the tumor board discussion.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the plan should be 'ready for Monday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a board-ready, clinician-facing package must be available before the Monday 7:00 AM liver tumor board so she can present it during case discussion.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the simulation and optimization outputs can be generated and uploaded any time by Monday evening, because the phrase refers to calendar-day delivery of the technical work product.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In hospital planning talk, saying something is 'for Monday' sounds fully specific because both people anchor to their own routine deadline convention; neither expects the other to need the exact hour spelled out.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the model should 'account for the vessels around the lesion.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this includes all clinically relevant nearby vessels that could create a heat-sink effect, including small branches she notices on imaging review or infers from local anatomy even if they are not separately segmented.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this includes only the segmented macro-vessels captured by the workflow, typically those above roughly 3 mm diameter, while smaller vascular effects remain folded into the generic perfusion parameter.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are accustomed to talking about vessel effects at a high level, and the omitted boundary between explicit vessel modeling and implicit perfusion treatment feels too technical and already-settled to restate.

misalignment_points.topic: What the 'planning packet' or 'final plan' is
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that Noah will send Elena the 'planning packet' or 'final plan' for the case.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects a concise clinical deliverable centered on one recommended probe placement, with annotated screenshots and perhaps a short backup note for awkward access.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects to send the standard modeling output bundle: three ranked optimized placements, uncertainty overlays, and supporting figures so the clinician can choose among them.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Each person's default deliverable is standard within their own practice, and the words 'plan' and 'packet' sound concrete enough that neither notices they are imagining different levels of curation and decisiveness.

turns.inner_thought: The segment VIII metastasis is the right first prospective case if we can make this look clean and clinically usable. If we're going to say the workflow is being used prospectively, I need something polished before the 7:00 AM Monday liver board so I can actually shape the discussion, not a technical file that appears later. I also want to keep the process light enough that it doesn't slow down case selection.
turns.utterance: I think the segment VIII metastasis that's likely coming to the Monday board could be a good first case to use the new planning workflow prospectively. How do you want to set it up so we can get a run done and have it ready for Monday?

turns.inner_thought: This is a sensible candidate: visible lesion, standard RF geometry, and enough time to run optimization and uncertainty if I get the data. For me, ready for Monday means I can deliver the technical outputs by Monday evening. I should keep this within the standard reproducible pipeline: latest CT, lesion mask, liver, and segmented named vessels, then run the vessel-aware simulation and optimizer without promising handcrafted clinical polish.
turns.utterance: Yes, that case makes sense to me. If I can get the latest CT and the segmentation inputs, I can run the vessel-aware simulation and the probe placement optimization on it.

turns.inner_thought: On imaging there is a small vessel cluster hugging the posterior edge that could absolutely matter for heat sink. When I say account for the vessels around the lesion, I mean that posterior little complex too, even if it's not a beautifully segmented named branch. I need to hear that this won't ignore the exact anatomy that worries me clinically.
turns.utterance: Good. On that one, there's a small vessel complex hugging the posterior edge of the lesion, so it's important that the model really accounts for the vessels around that side.

turns.inner_thought: As long as we segment the portal and hepatic veins in the usual way, the main convective cooling effects should be represented. I am not going to start manually chasing every tiny branch near the tumor; below the pipeline threshold those effects stay in the background perfusion term. That's the defensible and reproducible approach for a first prospective run.
turns.utterance: That should be fine. Once the portal and hepatic veins are segmented, the model should capture the main cooling effect, and I'll keep the usual perfusion treatment for the rest.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect, then he understands the vessel issue. Now I need to make sure this lands in time for board discussion. If I tell him to have the plan ready for Monday, surely he'll know I mean before the 7:00 AM tumor board, and what I need is a clinician-facing final plan, not a loose set of options.
turns.utterance: That's great. Then let's have the plan ready for Monday so I can move the case forward smoothly.

turns.inner_thought: Monday is workable if I do the segmentation checks over the weekend and finish the uncertainty runs that day. I can send the standard planning packet after the ranked trajectories are finalized. That should satisfy prospective use since it will still be generated before treatment, even if the board happens earlier.
turns.utterance: Yes, I should be able to send the planning packet Monday after I finish the uncertainty runs and rank the top trajectories.

turns.inner_thought: Good, so I'll have something concise to show at board: one recommended probe path, annotated screenshots, expected margin, maybe one backup if access is awkward. They do not want a modeling dossier at 7:00 in the morning. I need it to look settled and clinically actionable.
turns.utterance: For the board, I really just need the final plan with clear images showing where the probe would go and what margin we can expect.

turns.inner_thought: That's consistent with sending the full packet—she can look at the images and decide which trajectory she likes. I shouldn't collapse this to a single recommendation because for a first case I want to stay methodologically careful and show the top feasible solutions with uncertainty context rather than implying false precision.
turns.utterance: No problem. The packet will include the best three placements, the uncertainty overlays, and the coverage plots so you can select the one you prefer.

turns.inner_thought: Fine—he'll send the plan and I can pull the final recommended view into the board deck. My fellow can transfer the scan and I'll personally review the lesion and nearby vessels to make sure the anatomy is represented the way we need. As long as the packet is in before Monday morning, this should be smooth.
turns.utterance: Okay. I'll have my fellow push over the imaging, and I'll review the anatomy on our side. You handle the optimization and send the packet once it's ready.

turns.inner_thought: Great, we have a straightforward division of labor. I'll run the standard vessel-aware pipeline, avoid one-off manual tailoring, and deliver the usual modeling bundle on Monday. That should give us a clean first prospective demonstration without overstating certainty.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll use the standard vessel-aware pipeline and get the packet to you on Monday.
